lessons.title: A Systematic Approach to Performance Tuning

slots.practicalActivity: On your own SQL Server instance, pick one real AdventureWorks2012 report query (e.g., a join of Sales.SalesOrderHeader to Sales.SalesOrderDetail and Production.Product). Write down a vague initial complaint about it ("this report feels slow"), then apply this lesson's technique to turn that into a precise definition of slow with a specific duration threshold and business impact, and capture a one-time baseline using SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON plus the actual execution plan.
slots.deliverable: A short written baseline document for one real AdventureWorks2012 query: the vague complaint, the precise "slow" definition, the captured STATISTICS IO/TIME numbers, and a saved execution plan (.sqlplan file).

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same AdventureWorks2012 query baselined in the previous slot, walk it through the full measure -> identify -> change -> verify tuning loop, and for each of the four stages note which specific tool (SSMS execution plan, Query Store, a DMV, Extended Events, or a third-party tool) you would reach for and why.
slots.deliverable: A one-page workflow worksheet mapping all four loop stages to this specific query, with the tool chosen for each stage and a one-sentence justification for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Capture both the estimated and actual execution plan for a join-heavy AdventureWorks2012 query (Sales.SalesOrderHeader joined to Sales.SalesOrderDetail, filtered by a specific CustomerID). Number the operators in the order they truly execute (right-to-left, bottom-to-top), hover every connecting arrow to record the row counts flowing through it, and circle the single operator carrying the highest cost percentage.
slots.deliverable: An annotated screenshot or saved .sqlplan of the query's actual plan, with operators numbered in true execution order, arrow row counts noted, and the highest-cost operator identified with a one-sentence explanation of why it's expensive.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a parameterized stored procedure against Sales.SalesOrderHeader filtered by CustomerID. Execute it first with a low-order-count customer and then with a high-order-count customer, use sys.dm_exec_cached_plans and sys.dm_exec_query_stats to show the one cached plan now serving both parameter values, then apply OPTION (RECOMPILE) (or a plan guide) and compare the measured effect.
slots.deliverable: A before/after log showing the single cached plan causing a slow run for the second parameter value, plus the specific hint or recompile option applied and its measured effect on duration.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter lab: pick one more AdventureWorks2012 stored procedure with at least one parameter and, without new instruction, run it through this chapter's full workflow end to end: read the actual plan, check for parameter-sniffing symptoms, and decide whether a hint, a recompile option, or no change at all is warranted.
slots.deliverable: A one-page writeup of an independently diagnosed procedure, including the actual plan evidence that justified your decision.

slots.practicalActivity: On Sales.SalesOrderHeader, design and create one new nonclustered covering index keyed on CustomerID with OrderDate DESC in the key and TotalDue/Status in INCLUDE, for a query that filters by CustomerID, orders by OrderDate, and selects those columns. Capture the plan before (Key Lookup present) and after (no Key Lookup) creating the index.
slots.deliverable: The CREATE INDEX statement used, plus before/after execution plans showing the Key Lookup operator disappear.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a filtered index on Sales.SalesOrderHeader for one narrow, frequently-queried status value and compare its size to a full index on the same column. Then create a nonclustered columnstore index on Sales.SalesOrderDetail for an analytical aggregate query (SUM of LineTotal grouped by ProductID) and compare its plan and duration against the rowstore version.
slots.deliverable: Size comparison numbers for the filtered vs. unfiltered index, plus before/after duration and plan evidence for the columnstore aggregate query.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter lab: run the full index tuning workflow from this chapter against a table you haven't touched yet in this course (e.g., Production.Product) - find a real slow query against it, design one covering or filtered index, implement it, and confirm the plan improved.
slots.deliverable: A documented before/after index tuning case for Production.Product, including the query, the index DDL, and the plan evidence of improvement.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a query against Sales.SalesOrderHeader that wraps OrderDate in YEAR() in its WHERE clause, confirm via the plan that it scans instead of seeks, then rewrite it as a sargable date-range predicate. Separately, find one procedural (cursor- or loop-based) calculation against Sales.SalesOrderDetail and rewrite it as an equivalent set-based query.
slots.deliverable: Two before/after query pairs - a sargability rewrite and a cursor-to-set-based rewrite - each with plan or timing evidence proving the rewrite improved performance.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the same intermediate result set from Sales.SalesOrderDetail once as a #temp table and once as a table variable, and compare their plans and statistics. Then wrap a column in a scalar UDF inside a WHERE clause against Sales.SalesOrderHeader, confirm the plan goes row-by-row, and rewrite it without the UDF. Finally, batch an UPDATE against a large result set using TOP (n) in a loop instead of one giant transaction.
slots.deliverable: A comparison note on temp table vs. table variable plan/statistics behavior, the UDF rewrite with before/after timings, and one working batched UPDATE script.

slots.practicalActivity: Run DBCC SQLPERF('sys.dm_os_wait_stats', CLEAR), generate load by running several heavy AdventureWorks2012 aggregate queries concurrently in 3-4 query windows, then query sys.dm_os_wait_stats ranked by percentage of total and classify the top waits as CPU-bound (signal-wait heavy) or I/O-bound (PAGEIOLATCH-heavy).
slots.deliverable: A ranked wait-stats report (top 10, with running percentage) from your own clean measurement window, with each top wait type labeled CPU-bound or I/O-bound and justified by resource vs. signal wait time.

slots.practicalActivity: Query sys.dm_os_memory_clerks and Page Life Expectancy via sys.dm_os_performance_counters on your instance to assess current memory pressure. Separately, check ASYNC_NETWORK_IO wait time and sys.dm_exec_connections to assess whether any current session is network-bound rather than server-bound.
slots.deliverable: A short memory-pressure and network-wait assessment of your own instance's current state, with the specific DMV query and result used to support each conclusion.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter lab: clear wait stats, then deliberately reproduce one wait-type family from this chapter on purpose (force I/O waits with a large uncached table scan, or force CPU waits with several parallel aggregate queries at once), and diagnose which wait type dominates using only this chapter's methodology, without being told which one to expect.
slots.deliverable: A diagnosis report identifying the dominant wait type you deliberately induced, backed by the actual DMV output, confirming you can run the methodology blind.

slots.practicalActivity: Check sys.dm_os_wait_stats for PAGELATCH_UP/EX waits, confirm TempDB's current data-file count and sizing via sys.master_files, and if TempDB has only one data file, add 3 additional equally-sized data files per this lesson's sizing guidance. Separately, run a large sort/hash query against AdventureWorks2012 and inspect its memory grant in the actual plan's properties.
slots.deliverable: A before/after sys.master_files listing showing TempDB's file count and equal sizing, plus a screenshot of one query's actual memory grant with requested vs. granted memory noted.

slots.practicalActivity: Query sys.dm_os_buffer_descriptors to see how much buffer pool space AdventureWorks2012 currently occupies, and check Page Life Expectancy. Then create a Resource Governor workload group and classifier function that caps a test login's queries at a lower MAXDOP/memory grant than the default pool, and confirm it applies to a connection using that login.
slots.deliverable: A buffer pool usage snapshot for one database, plus a working Resource Governor configuration (classifier function + workload group) confirmed to apply to a test login.

slots.practicalActivity: Enable Query Store on AdventureWorks2012 with explicit options (OPERATION_MODE, QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE, CLEANUP_POLICY) rather than defaults. Run a parameter-sensitive procedure with two very different parameter values to generate two plans for the same query_id, then force the better-performing plan with sys.sp_query_store_force_plan and confirm forced_plan = 1 in sys.query_store_plan.
slots.deliverable: A query against sys.query_store_query/plan/runtime_stats showing two plans for one query_id, plus confirmation that a specific plan is now force-applied.

slots.practicalActivity: Use the Query Store "Regressed Queries" report in SSMS (or an equivalent sys.query_store_* query) to find any query whose average duration increased between two time intervals. Then check Query Store's current OPERATION_MODE and MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB to confirm it hasn't silently flipped to read-only.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or query result identifying one regressed (or confirmed non-regressed) query with before/after interval numbers, plus a check confirming Query Store's current operation mode and storage usage.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: without new instruction, take the query you force-planned earlier in this chapter and deliberately change the condition that made it beneficial (e.g., rebuild the underlying index so the optimizer would naturally pick a different plan), observe how the Regressed Queries report reacts, then decide whether to keep, update, or remove the forced plan.
slots.deliverable: A short log of the forced plan's behavior under a changed condition, with your documented decision to keep, update, or remove the force.

slots.practicalActivity: Check your instance's current 'max degree of parallelism' and 'cost threshold for parallelism' via sp_configure, compare them against Microsoft's NUMA-based sizing guidance for your own processor count, and adjust both with sp_configure/RECONFIGURE if they're still at defaults. Then run one query that goes parallel and one that doesn't, and explain the cost-threshold boundary using their actual plan costs.
slots.deliverable: A before/after sp_configure output for both settings with your written justification based on your own processor/NUMA layout, plus the two queries' plans showing the parallel/serial boundary.

slots.practicalActivity: Run sp_configure with show advanced options on to inventory your instance's min/max server memory and other instance-level performance settings, then write a one-page hardware/configuration assessment of your own machine (CPU cores, RAM, storage type) noting which settings are already correctly sized and which you'd change.
slots.deliverable: A complete sp_configure inventory of instance-level performance settings, plus a written hardware-fit assessment with specific recommended changes.

slots.practicalActivity: Create the dba.PerfBaseline table from this lesson, build a SQL Server Agent job that captures sys.dm_os_wait_stats and key sys.dm_os_performance_counters values (Page Life Expectancy, Batch Requests/sec) into it every 15 minutes for at least an hour, then configure one SQL Server Agent alert that fires on a specific performance condition (e.g., Page Life Expectancy below a threshold).
slots.deliverable: A populated dba.PerfBaseline table with at least 4 real captured snapshots, plus one working, tested Agent alert definition.

slots.practicalActivity: Research 3 real third-party SQL Server monitoring tools and note one concrete feature each offers beyond native DMVs. Then write your own DIY monitoring script combining at least 2 DMVs from this chapter (e.g., wait stats plus buffer stats) into one readable report query.
slots.deliverable: A short comparison table of 3 real third-party tools with one differentiating feature each, plus one original multi-DMV DIY monitoring script that runs successfully.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: A Slow Production Database

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the Meridian Outfitters scenario on your own SQL Server: create a dbo.Orders table modeled on the lesson's schema (OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, OrderStatus, OrderTotal, ShipDate), load it with a skewed dataset (most CustomerIDs with ~40 rows, one CustomerID like 48213 with thousands of rows), create the single narrow IX_Orders_CustomerID index and the usp_CustomerOrderHistory procedure exactly as shown, then run the Query Store baseline, actual-plan, and wait-stats diagnosis steps against both a normal and the wholesale CustomerID.
slots.deliverable: A working local reproduction of MeridianRetail's dbo.Orders/usp_CustomerOrderHistory, plus your own captured before-numbers (duration, logical reads, Key Lookup execution count) matching the lesson's diagnosis pattern.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab 1: extend the diagnosis - create two more synthetic "wholesale" CustomerIDs with high order counts, confirm each shows the same Key-Lookup-at-scale pattern, and check whether the PAGEIOLATCH_SH wait concentration you measured holds up when all three run concurrently in separate query windows, simulating peak call-center load.
slots.deliverable: A diagnosis log confirming the Key-Lookup pattern reproduces across 3 wholesale customers and gets worse under simulated concurrent load, with the supporting wait-stats evidence.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement the exact fix: create IX_Orders_CustomerID_OrderDate as a covering index (key: CustomerID, OrderDate DESC; include: OrderStatus, OrderTotal, ShipDate) on your reproduced dbo.Orders table, then drop the now-redundant narrow IX_Orders_CustomerID index.
slots.deliverable: The CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX statements executed successfully against your local reproduction, with sys.indexes confirming the old index is gone and the new one exists.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab 2: apply the same diagnose-and-fix workflow independently to a second slow query of your own design (a different filter/sort/output-column combination) against your reproduced database or AdventureWorks2012, without being told what the fix is first.
slots.deliverable: A second, independently diagnosed and fixed query with its own before/after plan and metrics evidence, proving the workflow generalizes beyond the Meridian example.

slots.practicalActivity: Re-run EXEC dbo.usp_CustomerOrderHistory @CustomerID = 48213 with SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON after the fix, confirm the Key Lookup is gone from the plan and duration/logical reads dropped by orders of magnitude, check sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats for any write-side regression, then write the five-section findings document (summary, symptom, root cause, change made, result) aimed at both a manager-level and a DBA-level reader.
slots.deliverable: A before/after validation log (duration, logical reads, plan evidence with no Key Lookup) plus a written two-audience findings document following the lesson's five-section structure.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab 3: write the same five-section findings document for the independent second fix from the earlier lab, then re-read it a day later (or have someone else read it) to check whether the "root cause" section is specific enough for someone else to reproduce the fix without re-doing the diagnosis.
slots.deliverable: A second completed findings document for the lab-2 fix, plus a one-paragraph self-review confirming it's specific enough for someone else to act on.

slots.practicalActivity: Assemble the Meridian Outfitters capstone (scenario, diagnosis, fix, validation, documentation) into a single portfolio write-up, then write and rehearse a 90-second verbal answer to "tell me about a performance problem you solved" that names the specific bottleneck, the specific fix, and the specific verified result.
slots.deliverable: A portfolio-ready capstone document covering the full arc, plus a rehearsed, timed 90-second spoken answer ready for a real interview.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can diagnose a real SQL Server performance problem using execution plans, index design, wait statistics, and Query Store, and implement and verify a targeted fix end to end - not just recognize that a query "feels slow."
